title: Beverly and the Prop Job

jokes.text: In 1609, when galileo first made this telescope... it was made of salami.
jokes.setup: Portentous historical narration about Galileo inventing the telescope — the audience expects a factual sketch premise.
jokes.punchline: The telescope was made of salami. The ridiculous material subverts the gravity of the historical framing.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist premise — the salami telescope is a genuinely funny concept, economically delivered. The comedy comes from the total incongruity of the material. Not uniquely Larry-specific, but it works as a sketch opener.

dialogue.line: it was made of salami.

jokes.text: Well, I can see the morta della constellation. And the planet bologna. Oh, and there goes the entire 'piccoloaf' galaxy.
jokes.setup: Larry peers through the salami telescope and describes what he sees in the heavens.
jokes.punchline: All celestial bodies are Italian deli meats/terms — morta della, bologna, and the invented 'piccoloaf' galaxy (piccolo + loaf).
jokes.explanation: The escalating deli-meat astronomy jokes build nicely. 'Piccoloaf' is the best of the three — a portmanteau that actually sounds astronomical while being a deli reference. The escalation structure earns a slightly bigger laugh each time.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: Hey... buona notte. That's-a nice suit.

jokes.text: Mmm... God, this salami stinks.
jokes.setup: Larry is performing a historical sketch while looking through a salami telescope on a live TV show.
jokes.punchline: He breaks from character to note the salami stinks — an ad-lib that punctures the artifice of the sketch entirely.
jokes.explanation: The beauty of this joke is its economy — four words that completely derail the sketch. It's also deeply character-specific: Larry's vanity and comfort always override professionalism. The ad-lib sets up the entire episode's B-plot about the prop job.

dialogue.line: Well, I can see the morta della constellation.

jokes.text: Well, that's 'cause you're looking through the wrong end.
jokes.setup: Larry complains the salami stinks mid-sketch.
jokes.punchline: The other performer deadpans that he's looking through the wrong end — implying the smell comes from one end being 'used' — a physical/scatological implication delivered with total calm.
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-structured punchline. The implication (one end of the salami is... worse) is delivered with professional deadpan. Good structure and economy. Docked for low character integration since any straight-man could say it.

dialogue.line: And the planet bologna.

jokes.text: Fortunately, for all of us, galileo ate that telescope and was forced to make the next one out of metal.
jokes.setup: The sketch wraps up the salami telescope premise.
jokes.punchline: Galileo ate the telescope — treating the absurd premise with straight historical-documentary delivery makes the escalation land harder.
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the sketch. The deadpan delivery of 'galileo ate that telescope' follows the internal logic of the absurd premise. Slightly bloated with 'and was forced to make the next one out of metal' — the button could be tighter.

dialogue.line: Oh, and there goes the entire 'piccoloaf' galaxy.

jokes.text: That thing he said about the salami stinking totally confused me and threw me off for the whole show.
jokes.setup: Post-show debrief. Hank is complaining about Larry's ad-lib during the sketch.
jokes.punchline: Hank claims he was 'confused and thrown off for the whole show' by a four-word ad-lib — revealing his extreme fragility and self-centeredness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank self-absorption. Only Jeffrey Tambor's specific brand of wounded professional vanity makes this land. His inability to adapt to a minor disruption says everything about his character. High character integration score.

dialogue.line: Mmm... God, this salami stinks.

jokes.text: I smelled the stench. I didn't think it was coming from the salami. Well, where did you think it was coming from? From you.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to defend himself by saying he smelled the stench too but didn't know where it came from.
jokes.punchline: Hank says he thought the stench was coming from Larry himself.
jokes.explanation: The setup/punchline is crisp and the insult lands with the specific quality of a long-time colleague who has stored up resentment. Hank's delivery of 'From you' has genuine bite. Well-structured, economical, character-specific.

dialogue.line: Well, that's 'cause you're looking through the wrong end.

jokes.text: The substitute couldn't find a proper salami, and he grabbed one off the set of The Price Is Right. It must have been 10 years old.
jokes.setup: Artie explains the prop disaster — the substitute propmaster couldn't find a good salami.
jokes.punchline: He grabbed one from The Price Is Right, implying the long-running game show has decade-old prop food rotting on set.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original industry-insider joke. The idea of The Price Is Right hoarding ancient prop food is a specific, smart showbiz observation. Sets up the Bob Barker punchline perfectly. Good structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Evidently, Bob barker has no remaining sense of smell.

jokes.text: Evidently, Bob Barker has no remaining sense of smell. Evidently not, or he would have stayed away from Dian Parkinson.
jokes.setup: Artie notes that the 10-year-old Price Is Right salami must mean Bob Barker can't smell.
jokes.punchline: Larry riffs that if Barker could smell, he'd have stayed away from Dian Parkinson — a reference to the sexual harassment lawsuit Parkinson filed against Barker.
jokes.explanation: Sharp celebrity scandal riff. The construction is elegant: Artie's setup ('no remaining sense of smell') leads directly into Larry's callback ('would have stayed away from Dian Parkinson') using the sensory metaphor as a bridge. Industry-insider dark comedy at its best. The Parkinson lawsuit was very current in 1994 — this lands hard for a comedy-savvy audience. High impact score justified.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. It's very difficult to find someone who can make a salami telescope that looks functional and that doesn't stink.

jokes.text: Well, I hear she wears a lot of cologne.
jokes.setup: After the sharp Dian Parkinson joke, the conversation could end there.
jokes.punchline: Hank completely deflates the edgy joke by offering the dumbest possible non-interpretation — as if Barker's proximity to Parkinson was just a fragrance issue.
jokes.explanation: Hank's obtuseness is perfectly calibrated here. His inability to follow a sharp double entendre and instead take it at literal face value is quintessential Hank comedy. The 'cologne' response is exactly dumb enough without being stupidly dumb. Great character integration — only Hank defuses a sharp joke this way.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Artie, I don't smell, do I?

jokes.text: It's very difficult to find someone who can make a salami telescope that looks functional and that doesn't stink.
jokes.setup: Discussing the difficulty of finding a new propmaster.
jokes.punchline: Artie states the qualification criteria for the job with complete professional seriousness — as if 'functional-looking salami telescope construction' is a standard industry skill.
jokes.explanation: Artie's deadpan professionalism applied to the absurd salami problem is a good character note. The comedy comes from treating the ludicrous prop problem with the gravity of a union negotiation.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: 9:00? That's too late. I can change it to 8:00.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ahem. 8:30?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 9:00 sounds right. All right.

jokes.text: Larry, this is my cousin Clyde from Baltimore.
jokes.setup: Beverly introduces her cousin Clyde to Larry in the middle of the workday backstage.
jokes.punchline: Larry barely acknowledges this, immediately pivoting to being starved and needing food — treating a personal introduction as an interruption.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Larry's narcissistic inattention to anyone who doesn't serve his immediate needs is on display. The joke is mild and more of a character beat than a proper laugh-getter, but it establishes the dynamic needed for the episode.

dialogue.line: They have an umbrella cockatoo that already says, 'hello, daddy.'

jokes.text: 9:00? That's too late. / I can change it to 8:00. / 8:30? / Well... 8:30. / 9:00 sounds right.
jokes.setup: Beverly has made dinner reservations at 9:00. Larry pushes back; Beverly offers 8:00; Larry counters with 8:30; they settle on 8:30, then Larry immediately agrees 9:00 sounds right.
jokes.punchline: After negotiating down from 9:00, through 8:00, to 8:30 — Larry declares 9:00 sounds right, completing a full circle of indecision.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured micro-comedy sequence. The rapid back-and-forth escalates and then collapses in a circle, perfectly illustrating Larry's anxiety-driven indecisiveness. The structure is airtight — set up, negotiate, counter, arrive exactly where you started. Strong character integration: this is very specifically Larry's neurotic relationship with his own preferences.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Tasmanian two tufted canary has a lovely bel canto. ♪br-r-r-r-r ♪ ♪r-r-roo-roo ♪

jokes.text: They have an umbrella cockatoo that already says, 'hello, daddy.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is reporting on her search for a bird that can sing Larry to sleep.
jokes.punchline: The bird says 'hello, daddy' — an oddly intimate phrase for a bird, delivered by Beverly with professional matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the strangeness of 'hello, daddy' as a selling point and Beverly reporting it with zero affect, as if this is perfectly normal information. Mild but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I honestly don't want to see Leno get one fucking new viewer just because they disagree with my stand on affirmative action and don't know his opinion about anything.

jokes.text: I can't take a political stand publicly, Beverly. It'll alienate some of my audience, and I honestly don't want to see Leno get one fucking new viewer just because they disagree with my stand on affirmative action and don't know his opinion about anything.
jokes.setup: Larry explains why he can't sign the affirmative action petition.
jokes.punchline: His stated reason has nothing to do with ethics or principle — it's entirely about the ratings competition with Leno, delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first great joke. Larry's refusal to support affirmative action is entirely framed as a Leno ratings calculation — and the parenthetical dig at Leno ('don't know his opinion about anything') is perfectly embedded. It's character-specific in the deepest way: Larry's defining trait is that every moral calculation passes through his ratings anxiety first. The line is long but earns every word. The Leno dig has a quality of genuine industry insider truth. Comparable in quality to an 8+ anchor moment.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Um, do you want Mexican food or Japanese food tonight?

jokes.text: And Beverly, by the way, Tatiana — I have a date with her Friday, and she likes green, so would you make sure to get my green shirt?
jokes.setup: Larry has just awkwardly declined to sign Beverly's affirmative action petition and expressed vague support.
jokes.punchline: Immediately pivots to asking Beverly to prepare his date shirt — a casual reassertion of the assistant dynamic immediately after performing liberal solidarity.
jokes.explanation: The immediate pivot from performative liberal sentiment to 'fetch my shirt' is a sharp ironic beat. The comedy is in the gap between Larry's self-image and his behavior. Good character integration — this is exactly how Larry operates.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: This show is like the waltons. They got their little colored girl takin' out the garbage.

jokes.text: See? I told you he wouldn't sign it.
jokes.setup: Beverly had defended Larry to Clyde before approaching him.
jokes.punchline: Clyde's immediate 'I told you so' confirms his read of the situation was correct — the joke is the total vindication of the skeptic.
jokes.explanation: Functional but efficient. The joke is really the juxtaposition — Larry's elaborate 'I support it from way back' performance immediately followed by Clyde's correct prediction. Economy is the strongest element.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: You wanna be the only fly in the buttermilk?

jokes.text: Would you look around you? You are the only black person on this show. This show is like the Waltons. They got their little colored girl taking out the garbage.
jokes.setup: Clyde challenges Beverly about her position on the show.
jokes.punchline: The Waltons comparison — a beloved all-white wholesome TV family — applied to a contemporary late-night show with Beverly as 'their little colored girl taking out the garbage.'
jokes.explanation: Clyde's critique is sharp satire. The Waltons reference is inspired — it's specific, culturally resonant, and the image of Beverly as 'their colored girl taking out the garbage' is both funny and damning. This is the show doing what it does best: using comedy to make a real structural critique of the entertainment industry.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: Too much affirmative talk and not enough action.

jokes.text: You wanna be the only fly in the buttermilk?
jokes.setup: Beverly pushes back on Clyde's critique of her position on the show.
jokes.punchline: Clyde deploys the folk expression 'fly in the buttermilk' — the only black person in an all-white environment — with total conversational ease.
jokes.explanation: The expression itself is the joke — it's a great folk idiom deployed at exactly the right moment. Clyde's character voice is specific and the phrase is memorable. Slightly docked for originality since it's a pre-existing expression.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: He's gonna be askin' you to shine his shoes.

jokes.text: White liberals... / White hypocrites! — shouted in the backstage area as Beverly desperately tries to hush Clyde
jokes.setup: Clyde is ranting about white liberals being hypocrites; Beverly keeps shushing him as they're backstage at the show.
jokes.punchline: The comedy is in the escalation of Clyde's volume as Beverly's shushing becomes more desperate — the cringe of a private family argument being conducted in a professional space.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy structure — Beverly's attempts to silence Clyde only escalate his proclamations. The humor is in the incompatibility of Clyde's righteous frankness with the carefully managed social environment of the TV show.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Say, beverly, listen, you know those shoes the wardrobe department sent over? ...would you mind lacin' them up?

jokes.text: He's gonna be askin' you to shine his shoes.
jokes.setup: Clyde has just called Beverly a token; she pushes back saying she'll ask Larry again.
jokes.punchline: Clyde predicts the logical endpoint of Beverly's deference — shining Larry's shoes — presented as the reductio ad absurdum of her position.
jokes.explanation: Sets up the immediate payoff perfectly — the show cuts almost immediately to Larry asking Beverly about his shoes, making this one of the episode's best structural jokes. On its own it's a solid dark observation; with the callback it becomes great.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: Close enough?

jokes.text: Close enough? [Beverly and Clyde exchange a look after Larry asks her to lace his shoes]
jokes.setup: Larry has just asked Beverly to lace his shoes, immediately after Clyde predicted he'd ask her to shine them.
jokes.punchline: Beverly and Clyde share a silent look — 'Close enough?' — needing no words to confirm what just happened.
jokes.explanation: Two words that complete one of the episode's best sequences. The economy is essentially perfect — the entire argument between Clyde and Beverly, the prediction, the request, are all resolved in a glance and two words. The reaction beat is the punchline. This is the kind of joke that rewards rewatch because you can see it coming if you know what Clyde said, but it still lands even on first viewing.

dialogue.line: His skirt was at the dry cleaners, so there was a conflict. He couldn't do it.

jokes.text: Garth Brooks, Victoria Principal, Steven Wright.
jokes.setup: Larry asks who's on the show tonight.
jokes.punchline: The guest list is announced with total matter-of-factness — the comedy is in Steven Wright appearing alongside Garth Brooks and Victoria Principal as if this is a perfectly normal combination.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke from the incongruity of the guest list. Not really a constructed joke so much as a show-world texture moment. Low craft scores because it requires no writing skill — the absurdity is just in the names.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Because black people find Larry to be white.

jokes.text: His skirt was at the dry cleaners, so there was a conflict. He couldn't do it.
jokes.setup: Beverly notes they had Patrick Swayze on in his skirt (To Wong Foo) and wonders why they didn't have Wesley Snipes (also in drag in that film).
jokes.punchline: Paula deadpans that Wesley Snipes's skirt was at the dry cleaners — treating the drag costume as a logistical scheduling conflict.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of a celebrity scheduling conflict involving a dry-cleaned drag skirt is perfectly Larry Sanders. The economy is strong — the joke is entirely in treating the absurd as logistical. Good originality for 1995.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You want me to turn gay, don't you?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Oh... yes, please. Make all of San Francisco's dreams come true.

jokes.text: Because black people find Larry to be white.
jokes.setup: Beverly sincerely asks Paula why they don't have more black guests on the show.
jokes.punchline: Paula's answer is completely matter-of-fact and devastatingly on point: black people find Larry to be 'white' — meaning culturally square, not racially white, but the double meaning is loaded.
jokes.explanation: Six words. One of the best lines in the episode. The joke works on multiple levels: it's a factual answer to a booking question, a brutal character assessment of Larry, a meta-commentary on late-night TV demographics, and it has the double meaning of Larry being literally white AND culturally 'white.' Paula's complete absence of hesitation or irony makes it land harder. Economy is essentially perfect. This is the kind of line that gets quoted. Comparable to an 8+ anchor example — sharp, original, devastatingly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Oh, well, Larry won't hire them. I mean, personally, I think it's terrible. I think it's unfortunate and embarrassing for all of us, but, as Larry said, in the super-secret memo, 'if it ain't white, it ain't right.'

jokes.text: Am I unattractive? / No. I think you're very attractive. / Good. Am I unpleasant? Am I unsuccessful? Am I... unsexy? / No. I think you're very sexy.
jokes.setup: Hank is fishing for validation from a female colleague, running through a checklist of his qualities.
jokes.punchline: The escalating 'un-' questions reveal Hank's bottomless need for reassurance; the woman's reflexive agreement to everything makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Hank's insecurity is laid out with the systematic logic of a neurotic — the un- prefix applied to each quality is a nice structural touch. The woman's willingness to confirm everything (and Hank's instant suspicion of it) is a good double beat.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You are such an asshole, Phil, you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: You know, if you're writing an article, don't use my name.

jokes.text: Make all of San Francisco's dreams come true.
jokes.setup: Hank accuses the woman of wanting him to turn gay.
jokes.punchline: She deadpans that him turning gay would make all of San Francisco's dreams come true — playing along with the absurdity while insulting him.
jokes.explanation: Good comeback line. The geographic specificity of San Francisco adds color, and the implication (everyone would benefit from Hank being gay and thus unavailable to women) is a solid burn. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: It's just Larry hogs all the freebies.

jokes.text: What these women don't know is that I'm just a nice guy. / That's right.
jokes.setup: Hank's self-assessment after the exchange about his attractiveness.
jokes.punchline: He declares himself 'just a nice guy' with total sincerity, immediately confirmed by the woman with the flatness of someone who does not believe this at all.
jokes.explanation: The 'nice guy' self-identification is an ironic classic — the show makes clear through the surrounding material that Hank is not a nice guy, and the woman's 'That's right' is either agreement that confuses him or sarcasm he misses entirely. Either reading is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: She's in love with wesley snipes.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, he's really cute, but I... excuse me.

jokes.text: When did it get so fucking hard to get laid in this town?
jokes.setup: Hank is told that Wendy 'will see him in June' — a polite rejection.
jokes.punchline: Hank's existential complaint frames his sexual failures as a civic mystery, not a personal failing.
jokes.explanation: Strong Hank line. His framing — 'in this town' — externalizes the problem onto the city rather than his own behavior. The bewilderment is authentic to character. Quotable because of the economy and the specific cadence.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: People always say that, but, you know, when I put the stuff on my face, I break out.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: She can get her money back.

jokes.text: Yeah, of course. I count many black writers among my closest friends. / Then why don't we have any black writers working here? / Oh, well, Larry won't hire them... as Larry said, in the super-secret memo, 'If it ain't white, it ain't right.'
jokes.setup: Beverly asks the head writer Phil why there are no black writers on the show. Phil claims to have many black writer friends.
jokes.punchline: Phil reveals 'Larry won't hire them' and then escalates to an invented 'super-secret memo' with the slogan 'If it ain't white, it ain't right.'
jokes.explanation: Phil's trajectory from 'many black writer friends' to gleefully inventing a racist memo attributed to Larry is a great character move. The 'super-secret memo' device is a nice absurdist touch, and the rhyming slogan is memorably trashy. The joke works because Phil seems to relish saying it while disclaiming responsibility.

dialogue.line: It's a fruit phone. Put the banana up to your ear.

jokes.text: Yeah. You know, if you're writing an article, don't use my name.
jokes.setup: Beverly calls Phil an asshole for the racist memo joke.
jokes.punchline: Phil's response is not to apologize but to ask that he not be quoted if she's writing an article — treating the conversation as if it's a press interview about the show's racism.
jokes.explanation: Phil's coda is perfect. Rather than apologizing or explaining himself, he pivots to source protection — as if Beverly might be a journalist. It reveals his self-awareness that what he said was printably bad, while showing zero remorse. Good economy, strong character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well... if you mean can he make a salami telescope, yeah, I think so.

jokes.text: Oh, of course not, no. This is just information I wanted for myself.
jokes.setup: Victoria Principal says she doesn't want to just talk about her products with Larry; Paula has been interviewing her about haircare.
jokes.punchline: Paula insists this is 'information I wanted for myself' — deflecting from the obvious fact that she's conducting a pre-interview on behalf of the show.
jokes.explanation: Mild but charming. Paula's transparent deflection is the joke. Works because it's so obviously false and she delivers it with complete composure.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Black people will never have as much experience as white people because up till 10 years ago, black people had no props.

jokes.text: It's just Larry hogs all the freebies.
jokes.setup: Victoria Principal notes she sent a large box of products last week.
jokes.punchline: Paula reveals Larry keeps all the celebrity freebies for himself — stated as if this is a well-known office grievance.
jokes.explanation: A small but well-observed workplace joke. Larry's star behavior extending to hoarding beauty products is specific and believable. Sets up the later scene where he gives Beverly the products as a parting gesture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I would like some yogurt.

jokes.text: Do you have skincare products for black people? / Yes. I mean my products are for everybody, all races. / People always say that, but, you know, when I put the stuff on my face, I break out.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Victoria Principal if her skincare line works for black people.
jokes.punchline: Principal gives the standard 'for everybody' answer; Beverly counters with the lived reality that 'people always say that' but the products cause breakouts — a gentle but real call-out.
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp piece of social comedy dressed as a product interview. Beverly's 'people always say that' is a real consumer frustration with real-world resonance. The joke is earned because it's true — the comedy doubles as critique of the beauty industry's 'universal' products. Victoria Principal's discomfort is the cringe element.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Baby, you're talkin' like it's Friday, and it's only Wednesday.

jokes.text: She can get her money back.
jokes.setup: Beverly has just said she breaks out from Victoria Principal's products.
jokes.punchline: Someone mutters that she can just get a refund — deflating Beverly's pointed critique with a consumer-service response.
jokes.explanation: Quick muttered aside that deflates Beverly's legitimate point with a bureaucratic response. Works on economy — four words that completely miss the point of what Beverly said.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yeah. Well, if Larry asks, tell him I went out to get his yogurt.

jokes.text: It's a fruit phone. Put the banana up to your ear.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the Beverly/Victoria Principal conversation, someone references a prop phone.
jokes.punchline: The phone is revealed to be a banana — a prop gag that intrudes absurdly on an otherwise grounded scene.
jokes.explanation: A background gag that works as absurdist texture. The banana phone isn't a fully constructed joke — it's more of a visual non sequitur — but it has an anarchic charm in the middle of a tense conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Forget our confusion. You know, we always had the impression that Hank was an only child.

jokes.text: Beverly, mon cheri, we need someone who's experienced. There are only a handful of black propmen in the union, and they're probably all tied up, but we'll check.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Larry about hiring a black propmaster.
jokes.punchline: Artie interrupts with 'mon cheri' — a patronizing Francophile endearment — then lists every possible excuse to not hire a black propmaster while claiming to be open to it.
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'mon cheri' is a perfect comic tell — the French affectation signals condescension dressed as warmth. His reasoning ('only a handful... probably all tied up... but we'll check') is the comedy of plausible deniability. Character-specific because Artie would never be directly racist but always has a reason.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's all connections. That's how your... your son got the job. Good-looking boy.

jokes.text: Well, if you mean can he make a salami telescope, yeah, I think so.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Beverly's cousin Clyde has experience with props.
jokes.punchline: Beverly, not knowing the full scope of prop work, answers the question with the only specific prop she knows about — the salami telescope from the sketch.
jokes.explanation: A superb callback that works as character comedy and structural comedy simultaneously. Beverly has absorbed 'salami telescope' as the definitive measure of prop competence. The joke pays off the episode's opening premise in a completely unexpected way. The understatement of her confidence ('yeah, I think so') makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Hello. Larry Sanders show. Who's calling? Larry's in a meeting at the moment. Could you please hold? Thank you and... cheerio.

jokes.text: Black people will never have as much experience as white people because up till 10 years ago, black people had no props.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Clyde has experience doing props for television.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's response reframes the question with a sweeping historical claim: 'up till 10 years ago, black people had no props.'
jokes.explanation: The best line in the episode and one of the series' great jokes. 'Black people had no props' is an absurdist restatement of very real industry exclusion — it's technically ridiculous (people have props) but historically accurate in the show business sense (black people had no props, no roles, no seat at the table). The double meaning of 'props' — physical objects AND industry recognition/credit — is brilliant. It's funny AND devastating. High originality, economy, and character integration: this is Beverly finding the exact formulation that is both a legitimate argument and a surreal joke. Comparable to a 9-point anchor moment.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm having a stroke.

jokes.text: I would like some yogurt. [Long pause]
jokes.setup: Beverly has just made a devastating argument about systemic exclusion. Larry is cornered.
jokes.punchline: Larry's only response is to announce he wants yogurt — a complete emotional retreat from the conversation.
jokes.explanation: One of the great reaction beats in the series. Larry cannot engage with Beverly's argument so his self-protective neurosis retreats to the most trivial possible request. 'I would like some yogurt' is Larry Sanders in four words: avoidance, self-focus, and the comedy of a powerful man rendered helpless by a direct moral challenge. The pause that follows (inferrable from the stage direction) makes it even better. Economy is perfect — ten/ten. This rivals the 'snip snap' anchor for character-specific deflection comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, I see that talent runs like a cancer through the Kingsley household.

jokes.text: Beat after 'I would like some yogurt' — Beverly's reaction, implied silent stare
jokes.setup: Larry has just deflected Beverly's entire argument with a yogurt request
jokes.punchline: Beverly's unspoken reaction — what her face does — is the topper
jokes.explanation: The pause after the yogurt line is its own joke — Beverly's face saying everything the scene needs without words. Larry Sanders Show lives in these beats. The economy is perfect because silence here is louder than any comeback could be. High rewatch value because it's the kind of moment you want to see performed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: otherwise elly may will be cutting up your fruit and telling you how loverly the show was last night.

jokes.text: Baby, you're talkin' like it's Friday, and it's only Wednesday.
jokes.setup: Beverly says she can't work for Larry anymore.
jokes.punchline: Paula's response treats Beverly's existential crisis as a case of the Mondays — normalizing the desire to quit by pointing out it's too early in the week for that level of drama.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully specific line. Paula frames existential work crises as a Friday phenomenon — implying that whatever Beverly is feeling is valid, just badly timed. The line has a warm, funny wisdom to it. High quotability because the concept transfers perfectly to real life.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have... I, honestly, I have no more niks, and I use a paring knife.

jokes.text: Tell him I went out to get his yogurt.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Paula to cover for her while she goes to interview at Arsenio's company.
jokes.punchline: The cover story Beverly invents is fetching Larry's yogurt — the exact request he made when he was dodging her arguments. The yogurt has become the symbol of her servitude.
jokes.explanation: Superb callback construction. The yogurt request that ended Beverly's argument with Larry now becomes the excuse she uses to escape him. The writers have turned a single throwaway line into a recurring symbol of Beverly's trapped position. This is craft-level callback writing — not just repetition, but deepened meaning on repetition.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: if it's a weeknight.

jokes.text: Forget our confusion. You know, we always had the impression that Hank was an only child.
jokes.setup: Hank suddenly produces a 'sister' Wendy and brings her in to meet Larry and Artie for the prop job.
jokes.punchline: Artie deadpans that they had always believed Hank was an only child — implying Wendy's existence is new and suspicious.
jokes.explanation: Artie's perfectly delivered skepticism about Wendy being Hank's sister is excellent character comedy. The payoff — that she's later revealed to be someone Hank was 'dry-humping under the bleachers' — makes this rewatch gold. Artie's instinct is correct from the start.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: you must just go home and rub cash on your face.

jokes.text: Oh, God, I don't have a resumé. / Hank said you didn't need one. / Hank.
jokes.setup: Artie asks to see Wendy's resumé; she reveals she doesn't have one because Hank told her she didn't need one.
jokes.punchline: Larry and Artie's shared single-word response — 'Hank.' — delivered as if this explains everything.
jokes.explanation: One word does everything. 'Hank.' is the complete sentence. The joke works because the audience knows Hank well enough that his name as a punchline explains the entire situation. The economy is essentially perfect — ten characters to encapsulate Hank's entire character. Strong structure: the setup carefully builds the absurdity (no resumé, Hank said don't bother) and the punchline is one word.

dialogue.speaker: Victoria Principal
dialogue.line: Are you two married?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Now, come on. We know how this business works. It's all connections. That's how your son got the job.
jokes.setup: Artie is clearly skeptical of hiring Wendy via nepotism.
jokes.punchline: Hank defends nepotism by pointing out that Artie got his own son a job — calling him out with the same logic.
jokes.explanation: Hank's tu quoque is actually correct — Artie did use his position to help his son. Hank being right for the wrong reasons is a sharp character note. The joke is that Hank's hypocrisy in calling out hypocrisy is itself hypocritical, but he delivers it with complete confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Victoria
dialogue.line: Are you two married?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: OK, maybe she's not qualified to do props, but when Beverly leaves, she could be Larry's assistant.
jokes.setup: Artie is clearly not hiring Wendy for the prop job.
jokes.punchline: Hank instantly pivots to a new position for Wendy — revealing he came in with a backup plan and doesn't actually care about Wendy's qualifications, only her employment.
jokes.explanation: Hank's rapid pivot from 'prop job' to 'assistant' reveals that 'Wendy' was always about getting someone he knows into the building. The comedy is in how quickly he moves and how little he respects Beverly's job.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: It's like when I met Jack nicholson, I died. I mean, I started kicking everyone all around. People thought it was some sort of an earth tremor or something.

jokes.text: Hello, Larry Sanders show. Who's calling? Larry's in a meeting at the moment. Could you please hold? Thank you and... cheerio.
jokes.setup: To demonstrate her qualifications as an assistant, Wendy answers the phone while Artie and Larry watch.
jokes.punchline: She does adequately until the final 'cheerio' — an inexplicably British closing that makes no sense on a Los Angeles TV show.
jokes.explanation: The 'cheerio' lands as a perfect beat. Everything else is competent but the inexplicable British send-off reveals a character who is trying but not quite right. The comedy is in the small wrong note at the end of an otherwise passable performance.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's an elizabeth Taylor night light, and she just whipped it up in 15 seconds. ...And, by the way, this is actual hair.

jokes.text: Artie reacts to Wendy's phone performance: 'I'm having a stroke.'
jokes.setup: Wendy has just ended a professional phone call with 'cheerio'
jokes.punchline: Artie's clinical self-diagnosis — delivered as the only logical response to what he's witnessed
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie delivers medical catastrophe as professional assessment — 'I'm having a stroke' is the show's version of breaking. Four words, maximum comedy from an actor who makes everything look effortless. High quotability; the delivery is the whole joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Listen, not only is it ugly, it's a fire hazard. If Larry turned this on, he'd go up in flames.

jokes.text: I'm having a stroke.
jokes.setup: Artie watches Wendy answer the phone with a 'cheerio' while Hank looks at him for approval.
jokes.punchline: Artie announces he's having a stroke — his reaction to the surreal situation escalating to a medical emergency.
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn delivering 'I'm having a stroke' with absolute deadpan is a great Artie moment. The line functions as both expression of exasperation and a literal Artie-appropriate response to the absurdity. The economy is perfect. High character integration — only Artie, in Artie's voice, reacts to Hank's nonsense this way.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly's father
dialogue.line: $800 a week. Stick with Larry.

jokes.text: Well, I see that talent runs like a cancer through the Kingsley household.
jokes.setup: Hank asks for Artie's verdict on Wendy.
jokes.punchline: Artie's compliment — 'talent runs like a cancer' — is technically positive but medically horrifying; the simile reveals what he actually thinks.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great lines and a candidate for the best Artie line of the episode. 'Talent runs like a cancer' is a perfect construction: it sounds like a compliment ('runs in the family') but the simile — cancer — reveals his contempt. Only Artie can deliver a devastating insult through the structure of praise. The specificity of 'cancer' vs any other negative word is key — it's the right amount of extreme to be both funny and withering. This is what 9-point writing looks like: memorable, character-specific, economical, and original.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I came to your office, and you were wearing genie pants and a turban. I thought it was so hysterical.

jokes.text: Beverly's quitting. You better find an assistant ASAP, otherwise Elly May will be cutting up your fruit and telling you how 'loverly' the show was last night.
jokes.setup: Artie delivers the news that Beverly is leaving and warns Larry about the consequences.
jokes.punchline: The Elly May reference — the naive hillbilly from The Beverly Hillbillies — applied to Wendy as a replacement for the sophisticated Beverly.
jokes.explanation: The Elly May comparison is an effective pop culture insult. 'Loverly' (Beverly Hillbillies speech pattern) is the right specific detail. Artie's ability to compress his contempt for Wendy into a single cultural reference is strong writing.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I wish I could give you a big, hot kiss, but I know that would make you feel awkward.

jokes.text: I have no more nicks, and I use a paring knife.
jokes.setup: Larry is on set discussing Victoria Principal's shave gel during the commercial break or a prep segment.
jokes.punchline: He announces he uses a paring knife to shave and gets no nicks from it — presented as a product endorsement that reveals an alarming personal habit.
jokes.explanation: The paring knife as shaving implement is a specific and weird detail that makes this joke work. Larry's casual mention of using a kitchen knife on his face — as if this is normal — is great character comedy about his general incompetence with ordinary life tasks.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I haven't eaten anything but cereal for the last 3 days.

jokes.text: You are doing this on your face, right? / Well... if it's a weeknight.
jokes.setup: Victoria Principal is walking Larry through a skincare routine; she asks to confirm he's doing it on his face.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'if it's a weeknight' implies he only maintains his face on weekdays — or that the routine is so extensive he doesn't bother on weekends.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great line. The pause before 'if it's a weeknight' is everything — it suggests that on weekends Larry's face is either not his priority or he's applying skincare to other parts of his body. The ambiguity is the joke. The economy is nearly perfect. Character-specific: Larry's self-obsession about appearance combined with his inconsistency is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's why we haven't had him on. You're fun.

jokes.text: What are you worth? / What am I worth? / Let's see. What time is it? / You must really be worth a lot of money 'cause it's just... you must just go home and rub cash on your face.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Victoria Principal what she's worth (net worth); she deflects with 'let's see, what time is it.'
jokes.punchline: Larry riffs that she must be so rich she goes home and rubs cash on her face — an absurd image delivered with talk-show charm.
jokes.explanation: The 'rub cash on your face' image is the right level of absurd for a late-night joke — not too clever, not too dumb. It's also a good callback to the skincare theme running through the episode. Larry's talk-show banter is shown as genuinely competent here.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, hell, cut the crap. That's not your sister. I saw you dry-humping under the bleachers.

jokes.text: No flipping.
jokes.setup: Larry closes the commercial break teaser with 'we'll be right back with Victoria Principal.'
jokes.punchline: 'No flipping' — a running gag/catchphrase where Larry tells the audience not to change channels, but said with total deadpan authority.
jokes.explanation: A show signature. 'No flipping' encapsulates the entire Larry Sanders meta-comedy in two words — the show is a show within a show, and Larry's catchphrase is about audience retention, but also about the real HBO audience watching. Good meta-self-referential quality.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fucked by the black man again?

jokes.text: Listen, Victoria Principal just gave me all these haircare products and gels and creams and so forth, and I want you to have them, OK?
jokes.setup: Beverly and Larry are mid-show during a commercial break; Beverly is quitting.
jokes.punchline: Larry presents the celebrity freebies as a generous gift to Beverly — but Paula earlier revealed he hoards them. The irony is that he's giving Beverly the products now that he knows she's leaving.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Larry hoarding freebies makes this moment funny — he suddenly becomes generous when he wants something (Beverly to stay). The 'and so forth' is a nice bloated detail that reveals he doesn't really know what he's giving her.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Fucked by the black man again?

jokes.text: Thanks. Are you quitting?
jokes.setup: Larry gives Beverly the haircare products mid-show.
jokes.punchline: Beverly immediately suspects the gift means Larry is quitting — a complete inversion of who is actually leaving.
jokes.explanation: The reversal is elegant. Larry is trying to win Beverly back, but his gesture is so unprecedented that Beverly thinks HE must be leaving. It's a compact character joke — Larry doesn't normally give things away, so the gift reads as abnormal behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: You know how hard it is to work on somethin' that little? First your eyes, they start to water, and then the headaches creep up.

jokes.text: I was gonna talk to you about that tomorrow. / Instead you just bring it up right here in the middle of the show?
jokes.setup: Beverly confirms she's quitting; Larry is incredulous she's raising it mid-broadcast.
jokes.punchline: Larry's outrage is that the personal/professional crisis is happening at an inconvenient time — prioritizing the show over the human conversation.
jokes.explanation: Larry's complaint that Beverly is raising this at a bad time — when she was waiting for a good one — is classic Larry. His priorities are visible: show first, everything else second. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Clyde
dialogue.line: Did you ever think would heavy d would let hisself get that fat? I don't think I could let myself get that fat.

jokes.text: What do you mean you're gonna lose your identity? What does that mean? / Are you two married?
jokes.setup: Larry and Beverly are having an intense personal conversation mid-show, apparently close enough to the set to be overheard.
jokes.punchline: An oblivious bystander/guest asks if they're married — misreading the emotional intensity of the conversation.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed interruption that reveals the emotional intimacy of Larry and Beverly's relationship from an outsider's perspective. The 'are you married?' punctures the drama with a social misread that's both funny and character-illuminating.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Um, it's about clyde.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, what now?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Is there any way we could get rid of him?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: It's like when I met Jack Nicholson, I died. I mean, I started kicking everyone all around. People thought it was some sort of an earth tremor or something.
jokes.setup: Wendy is gushing about how attractive Larry is, comparing it to meeting Jack Nicholson.
jokes.punchline: She apparently responded to meeting Nicholson by 'kicking everyone all around' — an inexplicable physical response that was mistaken for an earthquake.
jokes.explanation: The specific absurdity of 'kicking everyone around' as a reaction to celebrity beauty is genuinely strange and funny. The earthquake comparison is the right escalation. Wendy's character is established as someone who operates on a different logic.

jokes.text: Listen, um, my mom's down in the car, and I was wondering if maybe Larry could come down and take a quick photo.
jokes.setup: Wendy has just been effectively rejected for both positions; Artie is wrapping up.
jokes.punchline: Wendy asks if Larry can go to the parking lot to take a photo with her mom — revealing she had an entirely different agenda beyond the job.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Wendy's mother is waiting in the car — for a photo op — is a good character escalation. The whole job interview was potentially just a pretext for fan access. Artie's response ('Why don't you go down and wait? He'll be right there') delivered knowing Larry will absolutely not go down, is perfect.

jokes.text: Artie, my sister made this. / What is it? / It's an Elizabeth Taylor night light, and she just whipped it up in 15 seconds. It was just amazing to watch her mind at work. And, by the way, this is actual hair.
jokes.setup: Hank produces a homemade Elizabeth Taylor night light as evidence of Wendy's creative talents.
jokes.punchline: The nightlight is made with 'actual hair' — an alarming detail delivered as if it's a selling point. Hank's pride in it is completely misplaced.
jokes.explanation: 'This is actual hair' is a great detail. The Elizabeth Taylor nightlight is funny enough; that it incorporates real human hair escalates it to genuinely disturbing. Hank's pride is completely out of proportion to what is essentially a cursed craft project.

jokes.text: Not only is it ugly, it's a fire hazard. If Larry turned this on, he'd go up in flames. Throw it away.
jokes.setup: Hank presents the Elizabeth Taylor nightlight as a potential desk piece for Larry.
jokes.punchline: Artie dismisses it on dual grounds — aesthetics and genuine fire danger — the second concern being very real if there's human hair in the nightlight.
jokes.explanation: Artie's dismissal is practically perfect. 'Not only is it ugly, it's a fire hazard' is a model of escalating judgment. 'If Larry turned this on, he'd go up in flames' is a vivid image. The 'throw it away' is the right capper — no deliberation, no negotiation. Pure Artie authority.

jokes.text: Could she play the flute for Larry? / No. / Well, we had a lady in today who can.
jokes.setup: Hank is trying every angle to get Wendy hired, asking if she has any additional skills.
jokes.punchline: Artie's response suggests there's been an actual flute audition as part of their assistant search — presenting 'flute skills' as a legitimate job requirement.
jokes.explanation: The flute bit is a great absurdist Artie moment. The implication that 'playing the flute for Larry' is a real criterion in the assistant search is funny — it suggests Larry's needs are so specific and self-indulgent that they now include live musical performance. 'We had a lady in today who can' is a perfect deadpan comeback.

jokes.text: Sometimes I get so confused and it's like, 'Am I over there because I'm doing a good job. Do they even respect me over there, or am I just a token?'
jokes.setup: Beverly is speaking (in what seems like a confessional/interview context) about her confusion about her place at the show.
jokes.punchline: The honest articulation of 'or am I just a token?' — what Clyde has been saying all episode — lands as both comedic and genuinely uncomfortable.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's moment of honest self-doubt is the episode's most emotionally grounded beat — and it's funny precisely because she's saying exactly what Clyde said, but has arrived at it herself. The callback to Clyde's 'token' accusation makes it richer.

jokes.text: Let's not have David Duchovny on anymore. I literally don't have anything left to say to the guy.
jokes.setup: Larry is reviewing flowers Beverly sent; the scene is a moment of quiet backstage business.
jokes.punchline: Larry's declaration that he's exhausted his conversational material with Duchovny — said with complete finality — is an absurd showbiz complaint.
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry-insider joke. The idea that Larry has run out of things to say to a specific celebrity — and the solution is to simply never have him on again — is a perfect encapsulation of late-night TV dynamics. The specificity of 'David Duchovny' (a very 1995 name) dates it charmingly but the dynamic is timeless.

jokes.text: Beverly's letter: 'I remember the first day I interviewed for the job with you. I came to your office, and you were wearing genie pants and a turban.'
jokes.setup: Larry reads Beverly's goodbye letter aloud.
jokes.punchline: The letter reveals that Larry was wearing genie pants and a turban during the job interview — an absurd detail about his fashion history that is apparently a cherished memory.
jokes.explanation: The genie pants and turban is a perfect absurd biographical detail. The comedy is layered: it tells us about a specific eccentric moment in Larry's past, Beverly found it charming rather than off-putting, and Larry presumably doesn't remember or doesn't find it strange. The image is vivid and specific.

jokes.text: I remember those genie pants. / Keep reading.
jokes.setup: Beverly's letter mentions Larry wore genie pants and a turban to her interview.
jokes.punchline: Artie confirms he remembers the genie pants — meaning the pants were notable enough to be a shared memory — and Larry dismisses nostalgia to keep reading.
jokes.explanation: Artie's confirmation of the genie pants — delivered with the same matter-of-factness as if recalling a business meeting — is the right beat. The economy is excellent. 'Keep reading' cuts it off before it gets sentimental.

jokes.text: Is there a 'P.S.'? / No.
jokes.setup: Larry finishes reading Beverly's emotional goodbye letter — which ends with 'Love... Beverly.'
jokes.punchline: His first question after the tender letter is whether there's a P.S. — revealing his hope for something more, something additional, rather than processing what was said.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. Larry's response to a beautiful, heartfelt letter is to ask about a postscript — a hope that there's something else, something more, something Beverly withheld. It captures Larry's emotional incompleteness perfectly: he can't just receive the letter, he needs more. The question is also devastatingly funny in its smallness — the letter was profound and his question is about administration. Economy: ten out of ten. Character integration: nine out of ten — only Larry.

jokes.text: Larry tells Beverly he'll hire her cousin Clyde for the prop job. 'I checked wpjp. It's a great station.'
jokes.setup: Larry is making his peace offering to Beverly
jokes.punchline: Larry claims to have 'checked' wpjp as if it required due diligence — but earlier it was described as a small local Baltimore station, and Artie later calls it a 'local shit affiliate'
jokes.explanation: Larry performing due diligence he obviously didn't do — or chose to interpret charitably — as part of his charm offensive is a good character beat. Works best in context because we already know what wpjp is.

jokes.text: I haven't eaten anything but cereal for the last 3 days.
jokes.setup: Larry is pleading with Beverly not to quit, making his most heartfelt case.
jokes.punchline: His most personal revelation — after all the professional arguments — is that he hasn't been able to eat properly for three days, presumably because Beverly wasn't there to manage his meals.
jokes.explanation: A great character line. Larry's most emotionally honest plea to Beverly is not 'I'll miss you' or 'you're important to me' — it's 'I haven't eaten but cereal.' It reveals how completely dependent on Beverly he is, and how that dependency is his truest expression of need. The comedy is in the complete infantilization of a powerful man. Comparable to an 8+ anchor.

jokes.text: Laurence Fishburne doesn't make me laugh. / That's why we haven't had him on.
jokes.setup: Beverly says she doesn't want to quit — Fishburne doesn't make her laugh like Larry does.
jokes.punchline: Larry's response is to treat her compliment as a booking note — Fishburne doesn't make HIM laugh either, which is why he's not been booked.
jokes.explanation: A late-episode great joke. Beverly's statement is emotional — she's choosing Larry because he makes her laugh. Larry's response converts her personal compliment into a casting decision: he agrees Fishburne isn't funny enough for the show. It's both a misread of Beverly's moment AND a reveal about why Fishburne hasn't been booked. The character integration is nearly perfect — this is exactly how Larry Sanders processes emotion: through the lens of show business. Comparable in quality to an 8.5+ anchor.

jokes.text: Did Larry hire some black guy with no experience? / He worked for WPJP. / WPJP? What is that? / Excuse me — local shit affiliate.
jokes.setup: Hank learns Larry hired Beverly's cousin Clyde — a black man with limited TV experience — for the prop job.
jokes.punchline: Artie's dismissal of WPJP as a 'local shit affiliate' — delivered as if this is a standard industry designation.
jokes.explanation: 'Local shit affiliate' is a perfectly compressed industry insult. Artie's matter-of-fact taxonomy of TV station quality is funny — as if this is an official rating category. The dark comedy of the scene (Hank's outrage that a black man was hired) is contextually sharp.

jokes.text: How can you say that about my sister? / Oh, hell, cut the crap. That's not your sister. I saw you dry-humping under the bleachers.
jokes.setup: Hank defends Wendy as his sister; Artie is skeptical.
jokes.punchline: Artie reveals he saw Hank 'dry-humping' Wendy under the bleachers — confirming she is not his sister and that Artie has been watching this unfold with full information.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'Hank was always an only child' setup. 'I saw you dry-humping under the bleachers' is both the revelation (she's not his sister) and the most direct Artie has been all episode. The image of Artie impassively watching Hank dry-hump someone behind the bleachers and storing this information until the exact right moment is glorious. High originality, structure, and character integration — this is exactly how Artie works: he knows everything, says nothing until the time is right, then deploys it with maximum devastation.

jokes.text: Nice try, Hank. / Job's gone. / Fucked by the black man again?
jokes.setup: Artie has exposed Hank's scheme; the prop job has been given to Clyde.
jokes.punchline: Hank's closing complaint — 'Fucked by the black man again?' — is delivered as if this is a recurring pattern in his professional life.
jokes.explanation: 'Fucked by the black man again?' lands because of the word 'again' — it implies this is an established pattern in Hank's career. The line is dark, provocative, and revealing: Hank's racial resentment is presented not as ideology but as petty professional jealousy. Jeffrey Tambor's delivery makes it pathetic rather than hateful — which is the exactly right choice. Dark comedy at the show's characteristic level.

jokes.text: I have been working so hard today on this Barbie doll. I made her these 5 monster dinosaur outfits, and it was so difficult 'cause they're so little.
jokes.setup: Beverly is back at work; Clyde is there.
jokes.punchline: Beverly is revealed to have been making five tiny monster dinosaur outfits for a Barbie doll as part of her work day — a completely unexpected revelation of her backstage activities.
jokes.explanation: The Barbie dinosaur outfits are a delightfully specific absurd detail. The comedy is in the scale — Beverly's intense professional focus applied to tiny monster costumes for a doll. 'It was so difficult 'cause they're so little' is the right specific complaint.

jokes.text: I have to get Larry birdseed and a cuttlefish, and I have to order him some of those new underpants, the ones that won't leave a line when he's wearing his tennis shorts.
jokes.setup: Beverly lists her to-do list while Clyde criticizes her for being busy with trivial tasks.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'underpants that won't leave a line in tennis shorts' as a legitimate professional task captures the full absurdity of Beverly's job.
jokes.explanation: The underwear specification is a perfect encapsulation of what Beverly's job actually entails — intimate knowledge of and service to every physical aspect of Larry's existence. The detail 'won't leave a line when he's wearing his tennis shorts' is exactly specific enough to be very funny. Good character integration: the list (birdseed, cuttlefish, specific underpants) perfectly illustrates the argument Clyde was making all episode.

jokes.text: Did you ever think Heavy D would let himself get that fat? I don't think I could let myself get that fat. Well, I guess if they paid me that kind of money I could get that fat, but then I'd have to get a sweat suit and work it off because I have to move 'cause my apartment's so small.
jokes.setup: Clyde is still hanging around backstage while Beverly works.
jokes.punchline: Clyde's stream-of-consciousness about Heavy D's weight spirals into a personal calculation about whether he could afford to be that fat and would then need to exercise in a sweat suit in his small apartment.
jokes.explanation: Clyde's rambling stream-of-consciousness is a character comedy moment — he goes from celebrity observation to personal financial planning to apartment logistics. The spiral is charming but slightly too long to be as funny as it could be. Economy score reflects the bloat.

jokes.text: Well, this is working out pretty well, don't you think? I mean, he's doin' a good job. / Would you shut up, Clyde?
jokes.setup: Clyde has watched his prediction about Beverly's token status play out all episode.
jokes.punchline: Now that Clyde himself has gotten his cousin a job at the show, he suddenly finds everything is 'working out pretty well' — a complete reversal of his critical position.
jokes.explanation: The irony of Clyde — who spent the episode criticizing Beverly for being complicit in a white-dominated show — finding it all fine once HE has a relative employed is a smart structural joke. His critique was legitimate, but now that his cousin Clyde has the prop job, suddenly 'it's working out pretty well.' Beverly's 'would you shut up, Clyde?' confirms she sees it too.

jokes.text: Um, Larry, I have a favor to ask you. / Oh, excuse me. What? / Artie? Artie? / Um, it's about Clyde. / Oh, what now? / Is there any way we could get rid of him? / No.
jokes.setup: Beverly has just reclaimed her job; she now approaches Larry for a favor.
jokes.punchline: The favor is asking Larry to fire Beverly's own cousin — the one she just fought all episode to get hired. Larry's flat 'No.' closes the episode.
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode button. Beverly fought the entire episode — on principled grounds — to get Clyde a job, and now her first post-victory request is to get rid of him. Larry's single-word 'No.' closes a complete ironic circle: Larry, who wouldn't take political stands all episode, now refuses Beverly's personal request. The structure is near-perfect. The economy is excellent. This is the show at its best — the irony is earned through everything that came before, and the closing 'No' has exactly the right finality.

tmdb_overview: Beverly quits when Larry and Artie refuse to seriously consider her request that a job in the props department be given to a black person. Hank considers replacing Brian with a woman.
